paragraphs: PLM_BlockIndices stores a byte offset into the room's word-sized level data.
Halve it to a linear block number, then divide by the room width using the
SNES hardware divider. The quotient is the zero-based Y block and the
remainder is X. Six NOPs provide the divider's required result latency.
Scan the forty even PLM slots from $4E down to zero and fail with carry set
when none is free. A room population row supplies ID, byte X/Y and a word
argument. Convert Y * room-width + X to the level-data byte offset.
The ID addresses a bank-$84 PLM header: its first word is setup code and its
second word is the initial instruction list. Initialise the slot before calling
setup with X = header address and Y = slot; a successful spawn returns carry clear.
Run only while PLM_Flag has bit 15 set. Reset the shared draw-tilemap cursor
once per handler call, then visit occupied PLM slots from $4E down to zero.
PLM_Index is the durable current-slot identity because setup, pre-instructions
and instruction handlers freely reuse X. Empty slots are skipped.
Call the slot's pre-instruction on every eligible handler pass, then reload X
from PLM_Index. Pre-decrement the 16-bit instruction timer; only zero advances
the list. Starting from zero therefore wraps to $FFFF rather than advancing.
A list word with bit 15 set is bank-$84 code. PEA installs a synthetic near
return to the fetch loop and indirect JMP dispatches it; an ordinary RTS resumes.
A nonnegative list word is a frame duration followed by a draw-instruction
pointer. Save both, advance the list cursor four bytes and immediately apply
the draw instruction to level data. Then derive block coordinates and enqueue
the PLM's visible tilemap. Duration zero is not an immediate next-frame record:
the following pre-decrement wraps it to $FFFF.
Y begins after the command word. Rewind and save the sleep command as the
slot's instruction cursor. PLA discards the synthetic fetch-loop return, so
the final RTS exits Process_PLM through its original caller return.
The expired zero timer wraps to $FFFF on later passes until something wakes
the PLM by replacing its cursor or timer.
Clear the slot's ID so the outer handler treats it as free. As with sleep,
discard the synthetic fetch-loop return and RTS directly out of Process_PLM.
The parallel slot arrays need not be cleared because the zero ID owns liveness.
Treat the room argument as a global item-bit index. A negative argument
deliberately behaves as not collected. Otherwise convert the bit index to an
SRAM byte and mask, restoring the PLM slot X before testing the result.
A set bit follows the instruction-list target; an unset bit skips that word.
For a nonnegative room argument, set its global collected-item bit in the SRAM
mirror without disturbing neighbouring flags. Negative arguments suppress the
write. Item scripts perform this before granting the pickup and message.
A visible missile tank first branches to the empty-item path when its room-argument
bit was already collected. Otherwise it installs the pickup continuation as its
link target and a trigger-wait pre-instruction. The triggered continuation sets
the collected bit before clearing queued music and awarding five missiles.
A PLM draw instruction is a sequence of counted block runs applied directly
to LevelData. Bit 15 of a run header selects a column; clear selects a row.
The low byte is the block count and the following words are complete level
block values. Rows advance one word; columns advance one room-width row.
A zero word terminates the drawing. Otherwise the next two bytes are signed
X and Y block offsets from the PLM's original block. Sign-extend X and scale
it by two bytes per level word; multiply signed Y by room width and then by
two. The following run header begins immediately after that offset pair.
Use the native BG1 tilemap bases $5000 and $53E0 for PLM rendering, then
enter the shared renderer with Y at the current draw instruction. The second
base is intentionally $20 below $5400; later screen-half arithmetic accounts
for the split without masking the horizontal block coordinate again.
Start every draw-entry position from the PLM's block coordinates. Convert the
Layer 1 camera Y position to blocks and reject entries below its 16-row window.
Horizontal and vertical runs then clip their other axis before reserving VRAM
write-table space. Offscreen level-data changes therefore need no tilemap upload.
Clear the orientation bit to obtain the horizontal block count. Clip the run
against the camera's current 17-column update span, retaining a left-skip count
for its draw-data cursor. A run contained in one BG1 screen uses two VRAM writes
for its top and bottom tile rows; a screen-boundary crossing can require four.
Each level word uses its low ten bits as a metatile index. Multiply by eight
to select four word-sized entries in TileTable. Bits $0400 and $0800 request
horizontal and vertical flips: reorder the 2x2 quadrants and toggle tilemap
flip bits $4000/$8000. Each expanded block consumes eight staging bytes.
Clear the orientation bit for the vertical block count and require the column
to lie inside the camera's horizontal update span. Clip blocks above and below
the visible rows, then use two column-mode VRAM writes for the left and right
tile columns. Metatile flip handling mirrors the horizontal path's semantics.
After a visible run, restore the caller's X and advance past the run's source
words. A zero offset pair ends the draw instruction. Otherwise sign-extend the
next X/Y bytes relative to the original PLM block and render that entry with
the same clipping and upload rules.
Map a visible block row and wrapped 32-column block coordinate into the BG1
tilemap destination. Each block contributes two tile rows and two tile columns.
BG1XOffset bit 8 selects which $400-word screen half is currently displayed;
crossing column $10 and that scroll bit choose the opposite half consistently.
Build two VRAM write records for a run contained in one screen half. Horizontal
mode targets two tile rows; vertical mode ORs $8000 for column increment and
targets adjacent columns. Each record copies four bytes per metatile from the
bank-$7E PLMDrawTilemap staging buffer at its current shared write index.

lines.comment: Read this slot's byte offset into word-sized level data.
Convert the byte offset to a linear block number.
Supply that block number as the hardware-division dividend.
Use the divider's byte-sized divisor register.
Read the room width in blocks.
Start unsigned division by the nonzero room width.
Wait for the hardware divider to finish.
The quotient is the zero-based Y block.
Publish Y for setup, drawing and collision helpers.
The division remainder is the zero-based X block.
Publish X alongside the quotient-derived Y.
Preserve the caller's room-population cursor.
Use bank $84 for PLM headers and local code.
Begin at the last of forty even array-slot offsets.
A zero ID marks this parallel-array slot free.
Each PLM array entry is one word.
Report that all forty runtime slots were occupied.
Population X and Y coordinates are bytes.
Read the row from the six-byte room-population entry.
Use Y as the hardware multiplier multiplicand.
Multiply the row by room width in blocks.
Read the population's column byte.
Add X to Y times width for the linear block index.
Convert the block number to a word-array byte offset.
Store the level-data offset in the free runtime slot.
Read the population's word-sized room argument.
Keep the item flag, scroll pointer or PLM-specific parameter.
Read the bank-$84 PLM header address.
Claim the slot before running PLM-specific setup.
X now selects the runtime PLM slot.
Y now points at the selected PLM header.
Clear the PLM's extra per-slot variable.
Default to the local no-op pre-instruction.
The PLM header's second word is its initial instruction list.
Make the new instruction list eligible on the next handler pass.
Install a safe empty drawing record before setup.
Clear the instruction-command loop counter.
Publish the slot identity across setup's register use.
X becomes the PLM header address.
Y becomes the runtime slot offset for setup.
Call the setup routine stored in the header's first word.
Report a successful spawn regardless of setup's incidental carry.
Default pre-instruction and setup-safe local return.
Select bank $84 for near PLM code and data.
Test the master PLM enable flag without changing it.
Skip all PLMs unless bit 15 is set.
Restart the shared visible-tilemap queue for this pass.
Process the highest runtime slot first.
Preserve the current slot across dispatched code.
A zero ID means the slot is free.
Run this occupied slot's pre-instruction and script.
Recover the slot after arbitrary PLM code reused X.
Move to the preceding word-sized slot.
Run this slot's pre-instruction on every eligible handler pass.
Restore the slot after the pre-instruction reused registers.
Read the 16-bit frame timer for this PLM script.
Pre-decrement; zero therefore wraps to $FFFF.
Only an expiry to exactly zero advances the script.
Load the saved bank-$84 instruction-list cursor.
Fetch either a command address or a graphical duration.
Bit 15 clear identifies a duration/draw-pointer pair.
Keep the bank-local command address for indirect dispatch.
Y is the command's parameter cursor when it begins.
Create a synthetic near return to fetch another list word.
Dispatch the bank-$84 command; ordinary RTS resumes the loop.
Install the graphical record's frame duration.
Read its following draw-instruction pointer.
Make that drawing record current for this slot.
Advance past duration and draw pointer.
Save the next script cursor before drawing.
Apply the drawing record to the room's level data.
Recover the slot after level-data drawing.
Derive block X/Y for visible tilemap generation.
Queue the PLM's on-screen tilemap immediately.
Rewind from the parameter cursor toward the command word.
Recover the sleep command's own address.
Leave the saved script cursor parked on sleep.
Discard the fetch loop's synthetic near return.
Return directly from Process_PLM to the outer slot handler.
A zero ID releases this runtime slot.
Remove the synthetic script-loop return word.
Exit Process_PLM immediately after deleting the slot.
Preserve the runtime PLM slot offset.
Read this placement's global item-bit index.
A negative argument deliberately behaves as uncollected.
Convert the bit index to an SRAM byte offset and mask.
Read the byte containing this item's collected flag.
Restore the PLM slot before continuing its script.
Isolate this placement's collected bit.
An uncollected item skips the two-byte branch target.
A collected item follows the supplied instruction-list target.
Skip the target word and continue the visible-item path.
Preserve the runtime PLM slot offset.
Read the placement's global item-bit index.
Negative arguments opt out of persistent item tracking.
Resolve the SRAM byte and one-bit mask.
Read the current collected-item byte.
Set this item without changing neighbouring flags.
Persist the collected state in the SRAM mirror.
Test this placement's room-argument item bit.
Already-collected placements branch to the empty-item path.
An available item installs its pickup continuation.
Install the trigger-wait pre-instruction for the visible pickup.
Read this slot's current level-data draw instruction.
Y becomes the draw-data cursor in bank $84.
Read the PLM's original level-data byte offset.
Keep that origin for every relative draw entry.
X selects the first destination level word.
Read the orientation bit and low-byte block count.
Bit 15 set selects a vertical run.
A horizontal run uses the low byte as its count.
Advance from the run header to its block words.
Read one complete level-data block word.
Replace the destination block, including type and metatile bits.
Consume one source word.
Move one word to the right in level data.
A vertical run also takes its count from the low byte.
Read the next block for this column.
Advance one row of word-sized room blocks.
Peek at the signed X/Y offset pair following this run.
Any nonzero offset byte begins another entry.
A zero pair terminates the complete draw instruction.
Back up one byte to isolate signed X with an unaligned word load.
Move the X offset byte into the sign-tested high byte.
Sign-extend a negative X block offset.
Zero-extend a nonnegative X block offset.
Scale signed X from blocks to level-data bytes.
Apply X relative to the PLM's original block.
Keep the horizontally adjusted byte offset.
Use the overlapping load that places signed Y in the high byte.
Sign-extend negative Y.
Convert negative Y to its positive magnitude.
Accumulate a negative row displacement.
Zero-extend nonnegative Y.
Accumulate a positive row displacement.
Convert the signed row displacement to level-data bytes.
Combine relative X, relative Y and the original PLM block.
X selects the next draw entry's first destination word.
Advance from the backed-up cursor past both offset bytes.
Read the visible block row selected for this run.
Wrap the row within the 16-block-high BG1 screen.
Scale it by 64 tilemap bytes through the hardware multiplier.
Read the run's first visible block column.
Wrap it within the two-screen 32-block span.
Columns $10..1F use the second BG1 screen base.
Each block starts two tilemap words apart.
Add the first BG1 tilemap base.
Add the row product from the hardware multiplier.
Inspect which horizontal screen half is currently displayed.
Swap this column into the other $400-word screen half.
Add the pre-adjusted second-screen tilemap base.
Swap the second-screen column back when scroll bit 8 is set.
Leave the computed VRAM destination in A for the setup helper.
Add the vertical column-increment flag when requested.
Store the first row or column destination.
Read the clipped metatile count.
Each metatile contributes two word tiles, or four bytes, per record.
The paired tile row/column has the same byte count.
Use the shared bank-$7E expansion buffer.
Append after tilemap data queued by earlier PLMs this pass.
Publish the first staging pointer for metatile expansion.
The second half follows the first record's bytes.
Publish the paired staging pointer.
Both staging sources live in WRAM bank $7E.
